questions.question: What is Git and why do we use version control in software development?
questions.title: What is Git and Version Control
questions.direct_answer: Git is a distributed version control system that tracks every change to your codebase, who made it, and when. It lets multiple developers work on the same project simultaneously without overwriting each other's work. Version control is essential because it provides a complete history (you can revert any mistake), enables parallel development through branches, and makes code review possible through pull requests.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you actually use Git daily or just know it exists. They want to hear practical experience — branching, committing, resolving conflicts — not a Wikipedia definition.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only mentioning 'it saves versions of your code'. That's backup, not version control. The key value is collaboration, branching, and history.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the distributed nature — every developer has the full history locally. Compare to centralized (SVN). Mention your actual workflow: feature branches, PR reviews, rebasing.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Distributed = full history on every machine** — unlike SVN, you can commit, branch, and view history completely offline
- **Commits are snapshots, not diffs** — Git stores the complete state of every tracked file at each commit, optimized with compression
- **Branches are cheap pointers** — creating a branch is instant and costs almost no disk space; use them freely for features, bugs, and experiments
- **Staging area enables selective commits** — `git add` lets you choose exactly which changes go into a commit, keeping history clean
- **Pull requests enable code review** — no code reaches production without at least one other pair of eyes, catching bugs and sharing knowledge

Git solves the three biggest problems in team software development:

**1. History & Safety** — Every commit is a snapshot of your entire project at a point in time. Made a terrible mistake? `git revert` or `git checkout` takes you back. Deployed a broken release? Revert to the last working commit in seconds, not hours.

**2. Parallel Development** — Without Git, two developers editing the same file would overwrite each other. With Git, each developer works on their own branch. When they're done, Git intelligently merges the changes. If both edited the same line, Git flags a conflict for a human to resolve.

**3. Collaboration & Review** — Pull requests (on GitHub/GitLab) let the team review code before it's merged. This catches bugs, enforces standards, and shares knowledge. No code goes to production without at least one other pair of eyes.

**Why 'distributed'?** Unlike older tools (SVN, Perforce), Git gives every developer a complete copy of the repository including its full history. You can commit, branch, and view history completely offline. The remote (GitHub) is just a shared sync point, not the single source of truth.

## How Git Actually Works Under the Hood

Most developers use Git daily without understanding its internal model. Knowing the internals makes every confusing scenario (detached HEAD, rebase conflicts, lost commits) completely logical.

### The Three Areas: Working Directory, Staging, Repository

Git maintains three distinct areas for your files:

1. **Working directory** — the actual files on your filesystem. What you see in your IDE.
2. **Staging area (index)** — a snapshot of what will go into the next commit. Populated by `git add`.
3. **Repository (.git/)** — the permanent history. Each commit is an immutable snapshot stored here.

```
Working Directory    →  git add  →  Staging Area   →  git commit  →  Repository
(edit files)                        (prepared snapshot)              (.git/objects)
```

This three-stage model is what separates Git from simpler backup systems. The staging area lets you commit **selectively** — you edited 5 files, but only 2 are ready. You `git add` those 2, commit them, and keep working on the other 3.

### Commits Are Snapshots, Not Diffs

A common misconception is that Git stores diffs (what changed). It doesn't. Each commit is a **complete snapshot** of every tracked file at that moment. Git is efficient about this — if a file hasn't changed, the commit stores a pointer to the previous version rather than a copy. Under the hood, Git uses content-addressable storage: every object (file, directory tree, commit) is identified by its SHA-1 hash.

```
commit abc1234
├── tree (root directory snapshot)
│   ├── blob → src/App.java     (unchanged: pointer to previous blob)
│   ├── blob → src/User.java    (new version: full content stored)
│   └── tree → src/utils/       (subdirectory snapshot)
├── parent → commit def5678      (previous commit)
├── author: Alice, 2026-04-01
└── message: "Add user validation"
```

This snapshot model means **checkout is instant** — Git doesn't reconstruct files from patches. It just replaces your working directory with the snapshot from that commit.

### Branches Are Just Pointers

A branch in Git is not a copy of your code. It's a 41-byte text file containing a commit hash. Creating a branch costs nothing — no files are copied, no disk space is used.

```
.git/refs/heads/main           → abc1234  (latest commit on main)
.git/refs/heads/feature/login  → def5678  (latest commit on feature)
.git/HEAD                      → ref: refs/heads/main  (currently on main)
```

When you `git checkout feature/login`, Git updates `HEAD` to point to that branch and replaces your working directory with that commit's snapshot. When you commit, the branch pointer moves forward to the new commit.

This is why branching is "free" in Git — it's just pointer manipulation. In contrast, SVN (Subversion) copies the entire directory tree for each branch, making branches expensive.

### Distributed = Every Clone Is a Full Repository

In centralized version control (SVN, Perforce), the server holds the complete history and clients hold only the latest version. If the server dies, the history is gone.

In Git, every `git clone` copies the **entire repository** — every commit, every branch, every tag — to your local machine. You can commit, branch, merge, and view full history completely offline. The remote (GitHub, GitLab) is just a shared synchronization point.

```
Developer A           GitHub (origin)           Developer B
┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐
│ Full history │ ←→ │  Full history     │ ←→ │ Full history │
│ All branches │    │  All branches     │    │ All branches │
│ All commits  │    │  All commits      │    │ All commits  │
└──────────────┘    └──────────────────┘    └──────────────┘
    git push/pull         (sync point)          git push/pull
```

This means: if GitHub goes down for a day, every developer still has the full project history locally. If one developer's laptop dies, the full history exists on every other clone.

### Why This Matters for Interviews

Interviewers ask "What is Git?" not to hear a definition — they want to see if you understand the tool you use every day. Mentioning the three areas, snapshot model, and distributed nature shows you think at a deeper level than `git add . && git commit -m "stuff"`. The follow-up is usually about branching strategy, conflict resolution, or a time Git saved you from a disaster.

# Daily Git workflow — what you'll do every day at work

git checkout -b feature/user-login    # create a new branch for your feature

# ... make changes to code ...

git add .                              # stage all changed files
git commit -m "Add login form validation"  # save a snapshot with a message

git push origin feature/user-login     # push your branch to remote

# → Open a Pull Request on GitHub for code review
# → Team reviews, approves
# → Merge into main branch

git checkout main                      # switch back to main
git pull origin main                   # get the latest merged changes

# INVESTIGATION TOOLS — finding bugs and understanding history

git log --oneline --graph          # visual branch history
git log --since='2 weeks ago'      # recent commits
git log --author='Alice'           # commits by one person

git diff HEAD~1                    # what changed in the last commit
git diff feature..main             # what's different between branches

git blame src/App.java             # who last changed each line
# Output: abc1234 (Alice 2026-03-15)  public class App {

git bisect start                   # binary search for the commit that broke something
git bisect bad                     # current commit is broken
git bisect good v1.0               # v1.0 was working
# Git checks out the middle commit — you test, say 'good' or 'bad'
# Finds the culprit commit in O(log n) steps

# STASHING — save uncommitted work temporarily
git stash                          # save current changes (not committed)
git checkout hotfix-branch         # switch to urgent work
# ... fix the bug ...
git checkout feature-branch
git stash pop                      # restore your saved changes

- Git is distributed — every clone has the full history. SVN is centralized — history lives only on the server.
- A commit is a snapshot, not a diff. Git stores the complete state of every tracked file at each commit (optimized with compression).
- Branches are cheap in Git — they're just pointers to commits. Create branches freely for features, bugs, experiments.
- The staging area (git add) lets you choose exactly which changes go into a commit — you don't have to commit everything at once.
- git log, git diff, git blame are your investigation tools — who changed this line, when, and why.

questions.question: What is the difference between git merge and git rebase?
questions.title: Git Merge vs Rebase
questions.direct_answer: Both integrate changes from one branch into another, but differently. git merge creates a new 'merge commit' that combines two branch histories — the history shows exactly when and where the branches diverged and joined. git rebase replays your commits on top of the target branch — creating a clean, linear history as if you developed on the latest main from the start. Use merge for shared branches (main, develop), use rebase for cleaning up local feature branch history before merging.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand both approaches, their trade-offs, and — critically — when NOT to use rebase (never on shared/public branches).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying one is better than the other. Both serve different purposes. The dangerous mistake is rebasing a branch that other people have already pulled.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the golden rule of rebase: 'never rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared branch'. Mention interactive rebase (git rebase -i) for squashing commits before a PR.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Merge preserves history** — creates a merge commit showing exactly when and where branches diverged and joined
- **Rebase creates linear history** — replays your commits on top of the target branch as if you started from the latest code
- **Golden rule: never rebase shared branches** — rebasing rewrites commit hashes; anyone who already pulled those commits gets a diverged history
- **Interactive rebase cleans up before PRs** — `git rebase -i` lets you squash 'fix typo' commits into logical, reviewable units
- **`--force-with-lease` over `--force`** — after rebasing your feature branch, force-with-lease refuses to push if someone else pushed in the meantime

Picture a river (main branch) with a tributary (your feature branch) splitting off and rejoining.

**git merge** is like the tributary flowing back into the river at a junction point. The river now has a Y-shaped history — you can see where the tributary split off and where it came back. The merge commit is that junction point.

After a merge, history looks like main moving A, B, C, then a merge commit M that ties in feature commits D, E, and F—you still see the branch point and the join.

**git rebase** is like picking up the tributary and moving its starting point downstream. Instead of branching from commit B, your commits now sit on top of C — as if you started later. The history is a straight line.

Before a rebase, feature might sit as A, B, D, E while main advanced to C. After rebasing feature onto main, you get a straight line A through C, then replayed commits—same changes as D and E but new identities—so it reads as if you had always built on top of C.

**When to use merge:** When integrating finished work into main/develop. The merge commit documents 'feature X was added' and preserves the full development history.

**When to use rebase:** Before opening a PR — rebase your feature branch onto the latest main to get a clean history. Also use interactive rebase (`git rebase -i`) to squash messy commits into clean, logical ones.

**The golden rule:** Never rebase commits that exist on a remote branch other people use. Rebasing rewrites commit hashes. If someone else already pulled those commits, their history diverges from yours — causing chaos.

## Merge vs Rebase: The Visual Mental Model

The core difference is about **history shape**. Merge preserves the branching timeline as it actually happened. Rebase rewrites history to be a straight line. Neither is objectively better — they serve different goals.

### Merge Creates a Junction Point

When you `git merge feature into main`, Git creates a new **merge commit** with two parents. The history shows exactly when the branch diverged and when it rejoined:

```
main:    A ─ B ─ C ─────── M (merge commit, parents: C and F)
                  \       /
feature:           D ─ E ─ F
```

The merge commit `M` has two parents: `C` (where main was) and `F` (where feature ended). This is a permanent record that work happened in parallel. `git log --graph` shows the branching visually.

**Fast-forward merge** is a special case: if main hasn't moved since the branch was created, Git just moves the main pointer forward — no merge commit needed:

```
Before:  main → A ─ B      feature → A ─ B ─ C ─ D
After:   main → A ─ B ─ C ─ D    (main pointer moved to D)
```

Use `git merge --no-ff feature` to force a merge commit even when fast-forward is possible — this preserves the record that a feature branch existed.

### Rebase Replays Commits on a New Base

When you `git rebase main` while on a feature branch, Git takes your feature commits and replays them one by one on top of the latest main commit. The result is a linear history:

```
Before rebase:
main:    A ─ B ─ C
feature: A ─ B ─ D ─ E

After rebase:
main:    A ─ B ─ C
feature: A ─ B ─ C ─ D' ─ E'
```

Notice `D'` and `E'` — these are **new commits** with new SHA hashes. They have the same content changes as `D` and `E`, but different parents. The original `D` and `E` still exist in Git's object store (recoverable via `git reflog`) but are no longer referenced by any branch.

### The Golden Rule: Never Rebase Shared History

Rebasing rewrites commit hashes. If another developer has already pulled the original commits (`D` and `E`), and you force-push the rebased versions (`D'` and `E'`), their local history diverges from the remote. They'll see confusing merge conflicts or duplicate commits when they pull.

```
Your repo (after rebase):    A ─ B ─ C ─ D' ─ E'
Their repo (before rebase):  A ─ B ─ D ─ E

When they pull: "diverged — your branch and origin have diverged"
```

**Safe to rebase:** your own feature branch that nobody else has pulled.
**Never rebase:** main, develop, release branches, or any branch others are working on.

### Interactive Rebase: Cleaning Up Before a PR

`git rebase -i HEAD~5` opens an editor showing your last 5 commits. You can:

```
pick abc1234 Add user model
squash def5678 Fix typo in user model     → combine into previous
squash ghi9012 Another typo fix            → combine into previous
pick jkl3456 Add user authentication
reword mno7890 WIP: fix auth bug           → change commit message
```

This turns 5 messy commits into 2 clean, logical commits. Your PR reviewer sees a coherent story instead of your development journey.

Common interactive rebase commands:
- `pick` — keep the commit as-is
- `squash` — merge into the previous commit, combine messages
- `fixup` — merge into previous, discard this commit's message
- `reword` — keep changes, edit the commit message
- `drop` — delete the commit entirely
- `edit` — pause rebase at this commit for manual changes

### The Hybrid Workflow (Industry Standard)

Most production teams use both merge and rebase:

```bash
# 1. Create feature branch
git checkout -b feature/user-auth

# 2. Work, commit, push
git add . && git commit -m "Add JWT auth"
git push origin feature/user-auth

# 3. Before opening PR: rebase onto latest main
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
# Resolve any conflicts per-commit

# 4. Force-push the rebased branch (safe — it's YOUR branch)
git push --force-with-lease origin feature/user-auth

# 5. Open PR, get reviews

# 6. Merge PR into main (on GitHub: "Create a merge commit")
# This creates a merge commit on main — visible history of the feature
```

`--force-with-lease` is safer than `--force`: it refuses to push if someone else pushed to the same branch since your last fetch. This prevents accidentally overwriting a colleague's work.

### Resolving Conflicts: Merge vs Rebase

In a **merge conflict**, you resolve everything at once — all conflicts from all divergent commits appear in one resolution step.

In a **rebase conflict**, you resolve per-commit. If 3 of your 5 commits conflict with main, you resolve each one separately as Git replays them. This is more granular but can be tedious. If it gets messy: `git rebase --abort` takes you back to before the rebase started — no damage done.

# MERGE workflow — preserves history (use for shared branches)
git checkout main
git merge feature/login
# Creates a merge commit. History shows the branch.

# REBASE workflow — clean linear history (use for your feature branch)
git checkout feature/login
git rebase main
# Your commits are replayed on top of latest main.
# Then fast-forward merge:
git checkout main
git merge feature/login  # now it's a fast-forward, no merge commit

# INTERACTIVE REBASE — clean up before PR
git rebase -i HEAD~3
# Opens editor. You can:
#   pick   — keep commit as-is
#   squash — merge commit into previous
#   reword — change commit message
#   drop   — delete commit entirely

# RESOLVING MERGE CONFLICTS
# When both branches edited the same line, Git can't auto-merge:
git merge feature/login
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/Auth.java

# The file now contains conflict markers:
# <<<<<<< HEAD
# String token = generateJWT(user);
# =======
# String token = createSession(user);
# >>>>>>> feature/login

# Fix: choose the correct code, remove markers, then:
git add src/Auth.java
git commit                         # completes the merge

# RESOLVING REBASE CONFLICTS
# Same concept, but you resolve per-commit (not all at once):
git rebase main
# CONFLICT in commit D
git add src/Auth.java
git rebase --continue              # move to next commit
# CONFLICT in commit E
git add src/Auth.java
git rebase --continue              # done

# ABORT if it gets messy:
git rebase --abort                 # go back to before the rebase started

# THE HYBRID WORKFLOW (most common in production teams)
git checkout feature/login
git rebase main                    # clean up: replay on latest main
git push --force-with-lease        # update remote feature branch
# → open PR → team reviews →
git checkout main
git merge --no-ff feature/login    # merge with a visible merge commit

- Merge preserves history (good for auditability), rebase rewrites history (good for cleanliness)
- Golden rule: never rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared remote branch — it rewrites commit SHAs
- After rebasing, you need git push --force-with-lease (not --force) for your feature branch — it's safer
- Interactive rebase (git rebase -i) is your best friend before opening a PR — squash 'fix typo' commits into the real commit
- Most teams use a hybrid: rebase locally to clean up, then merge (with --no-ff) into main to create a visible merge commit
